title: Benchmarking Vector Databases: Throughput, Latency, Recall

questions.q: A benchmark asks for the 10 most similar vectors; the system returns 10 results but only 7 are genuinely in the true top-10. What is recall@10, and why is recall unique to ANN systems?
options: 0.7 — it is the fraction of true nearest neighbors actually returned, and it has no analogue in exact relational search
0.3 — it measures how many wrong answers were returned
1.0 — the system returned 10 of 10 requested
0.07 — recall is normalized by corpus size
questions.explain: Recall@10 = 7/10 = 0.7, the fraction of true nearest neighbors returned. Recall exists only because ANN is approximate — exact databases return the true top-K by definition, so the metric is meaningless for them.

questions.q: Recall, throughput, and latency form a triangle. What does that imply for benchmark design?
options: The triangle applies only to SQL Server
You must measure all three simultaneously at the same index configuration, or the results mislead
Optimizing one automatically improves the other two
Only throughput matters in production
questions.explain: Any two can be improved by sacrificing the third (e.g., more graph exploration raises recall but hurts latency and throughput), so honest benchmarks measure all three together — the recall-latency curve is the authoritative diagnostic.

questions.q: Why does the chapter call randomly generated vectors the worst case for benchmarking ANN indices?
options: Random vectors are uniformly distributed and do not cluster, so the index cannot skip regions and shows no benefit
Random vectors violate the distance metric
Benchmarking tools cannot parse random vectors
Random vectors are too small to measure latency
questions.explain: HNSW, IVF, and ScaNN exploit clustering in vector space to skip regions; random vectors are uniform in high-dimensional space and don't cluster, making them the worst case for ANN and producing recall numbers wrong by 5–15 points versus real embeddings.

questions.q: What happens in SQL Server if the METRIC in CREATE VECTOR INDEX does not match the metric argument in VECTOR_DISTANCE / VECTOR_SEARCH?
options: The index is used but with lower recall
The query returns an error
The mismatch silently disables the index and drops you to a full scan
SQL Server auto-converts the metric
questions.explain: The chapter warns that a metric mismatch silently disables the vector index, falling back to a full scan — one of the index-not-built traps that invalidates benchmark numbers, so index state must be validated before measuring.

questions.q: In the CI/CD benchmark script, what are the pass thresholds for recall@10, p99 latency, and QPS, and why should benchmark latency be measured from the client's perspective?
options: recall >= 0.99, p99 <= 10ms, QPS >= 10,000 — minimum production bar
recall >= 0.80, p99 <= 500ms, QPS >= 100 — because CI is approximate
recall >= 0.90, p99 <= 100ms, QPS >= 200 — to match vendor marketing
recall >= 0.95, p99 <= 50ms, QPS >= 500 — because that is the number your users actually experience, including network and serialization
questions.explain: The CI script uses RECALL_THRESHOLD = 0.95, P99_LATENCY_THRESHOLD_MS = 50.0, and MIN_QPS = 500.0, and the harness measures from the client side — including network round-trip and serialization — because that is what users experience.
